Researchers found that the compound, SD-208, which reduces scar tissue in organs, substantially reduced the release of extracellular vesicles, microscopic packages that cells use to carry proteins and other biological signals to neighboring and distant cells.

Science.title: How to spend $25 billion on science: OpenAI’s staggeringly rich research charity gets under way
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03015-0 Jacob Trefethen, who leads life sciences at the OpenAI Foundation, speaks to Nature about the organization’s ambitions to cure disease.

Science.title: 'Molecular movie' fills in blanks of how nonenveloped viruses infect cells
Science.summary: Viruses come in two major flavors—not chocolate and vanilla, quips Harvard Medical School structural biologist Stephen Harrison, but those enveloped in membranes, such as herpesvirus, influenza virus, HIV and SARS-CoV-2, and those that are not, such as poliovirus, HPV, rotavirus and adenovirus.

Science.title: Fossil long known as world's oldest reptile dethroned
Science.summary: For nearly 30 years, a small fossil from Scotland has been celebrated as one of the earliest known reptiles. A new study out today in Nature and led by researchers at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, is rewriting that story.

Science.title: Spatiotemporal clonal architecture of the newborn mouse forebrain
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11064-8 Clonal barcoding across the newborn mouse forebrain reveals developmental principles whereby glutamatergic neurons and astrocytes remain locally derived, whereas widely dispersed GABAergic (γ-aminobutyric acid-producing) lineages link neurons with oligodendrocyte precursor cells.

Science.title: Tracking the fin whale and the sperm whale in the Mediterranean
Science.summary: Where are the great marine animals of the Mediterranean, such as the fin whale, the sperm whale or the bottlenose dolphin? How does their distribution change over a few weeks? All indications suggest that these species shift between marine areas in a remarkably short time and over relatively small spatial scales. Some species, such as the striped dolphin, maintain a relatively stable presence in certain areas, while others, such as the fin whale, move and concentrate in different areas from one observation campaign to the next.

Science.title: Woman's 5-year struggle with balance and walking was caused by a 'one-in-a-million' disorder
Science.summary: A woman developed severe stiffness in her knees, along with a range of other symptoms. Blood tests revealed her very rare disorder.

Science.title: An amygdala to anterior hypothalamic circuit gates stress sensitivity
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11075-5 The anterior hypothalamic nucleus regulates negative valence in the brain, highlighting a new pathway that controls sensitivity to stressful events and signposting approaches to identify new circuit interactions relevant to mental health.

Science.title: Bacteria can make plant-based foods healthier for humans and animals
Science.summary: New research from the DTU National Food Institute and Aarhus University shows that microorganisms can be used to specifically alter the amino acid composition of plant-based foods, making them more nutritious and therefore healthier.

Science.title: Restoring hearing in people with a rare form of deafness
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02894-7 How a decades-long quest led to the first gene therapy for deafness caused by a mutation.

Science.title: AI ‘speech clock’ assesses how fast you’re ageing from your voice
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03106-y The pitch and emotional content of your speech are important predictors of accelerated ageing, researchers find.

Science.title: Scientists develop 'floating scarecrow' to protect threatened seabirds
Science.summary: New research has shown that a "floating scarecrow" developed by U.K.-based scientists and a repurposed bird-scaring kite can help save threatened seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets.

Science.title: Scientists in 1960 predicted Friday 13 November 2026 will be 'Doomsday.' Should you be worried?
Science.summary: In 1960, Science, one of the world's leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026. It predicted that on this future date—just over a month from today—the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself.

Science.title: Pompeii’s 2,000-year-old eruption just gave scientists a better clock for Earth’s past
Science.summary: Mount Vesuvius’ famous 79 CE eruption has given scientists a remarkably precise benchmark for dating events deep in Earth’s past. The improved technique could sharpen the timelines of volcanic eruptions, asteroid impacts, extinctions, and other major moments in geological history.

Science.title: Self-aligned optical microcomb emerging between octave-separated lasers
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11086-2 An architectural inversion shifts integrated optical frequency comb generation from outward broadening around a central pump to filling the spectrum between two octave-separated pumps through a self-aligned parametrically driven cavity soliton, enabling robust self-referencing for future deployable on-chip frequency and time metrology.

Science.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover just hit 5,000 days on Mars and sent back this stunning view
Science.summary: NASA’s Curiosity rover marked 5,000 Martian days by capturing morning and afternoon views that were blended into a striking Mars “postcard.” The panorama shows Curiosity, its tracks, and the enormous landscape surrounding Mount Sharp and Gale Crater.

Science.title: Type 2 immune history trains lung macrophages for viral disease tolerance
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11060-y Type 2 inflammation trains nerve- and airway-associated macrophages to confer disease tolerance against lethal influenza by limiting immunopathology and promoting tissue repair without enhancing viral clearance.

Science.title: Elena, Aris, Marcus: AI-generated ‘ghosts’ are polluting the scientific literature
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02991-7 The overuse of certain names has revealed the scale of fake experts on academic publishing platforms, say researchers.

Science.title: Function-preserving watermarking of AI-generated proteins
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10965-y SynthIDBio watermarks AI-generated protein sequences and structures while preserving function, enabling provenance detection and offering a proof-of-concept tool for biosecurity and information integrity.

Science.title: Ocean predator chemical cues could provide early warnings for toxic algal blooms
Science.summary: A team of marine scientists led by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, has developed a new approach to predicting harmful algal blooms (HABs), changing how oceanographers track these hazardous marine events.

Science.title: Dynamic protrusions mediate crawling motility in Asgard archaea
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11063-9 Anoxic live-cell imaging shows actin-dependent crawling motility and dynamic protrusions in Asgard archaea, providing insights into cellular innovations that may have contributed to eukaryotic evolution.

Science.title: Fluorescent sensors could help researchers see diabetes in action
Science.summary: Researchers from the University of Bath have developed fluorescent molecular probes that can detect changes in glucose levels inside living animals, giving scientists new ways of visualizing sugar uptake and studying diabetes, cancer and other metabolic diseases in whole organisms in real time. The findings are published in the journal Advanced Science.

Science.title: Clay tablets reveal how Babylonian students learned about their gods
Science.summary: When it came to religious education in ancient Babylonia, in what is now Iraq, students had a lot to learn, ranging from the names of gods to their divine characteristics. A new study published in the journal Iraq has taken a deep dive into ancient texts and surviving clay tablets to find out just how these traditions were taught in the classroom.

Science.title: Mouse study reveals magnetic nanoparticles' potential for ectopic pregnancy diagnosis and treatment
Science.summary: A research team led by an Oregon State University scientist has demonstrated in a mouse model a potentially better way to care for women facing the life-threatening condition of ectopic pregnancy.

Science.title: Groups of genetically identical fish follow different behavioral paths as they mature
Science.summary: Schooling fish have long fascinated us with their mesmerizing collective movements and seemingly perfect coordination. But a new study on clonal mollies suggests that this behavior is not innate. During their first days of life, the fish still display distinct individual behaviors, and it is only around one month of age that they begin to form cohesive shoals, developing the coordinated movements characteristic of the group. However, several shoals of genetically identical clones begin to behave differently after a few weeks.

Science.title: These optical illusions are why butterflies are so hard to catch
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03124-w High-speed footage of takeoffs reveal that the butterfly markings mislead the eye, making them harder to catch.

Science.title: Evolution of terrestrial anatomy revealed by a derived stem tetrapod
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11090-6 New anatomical evidence reclassifies Westlothiana as an aquatic stem tetrapod, showing that terrestrial limb adaptations evolved mosaically in transitional amphibious environments before crown tetrapods emerged.

Science.title: Peruvian mummies raise questions about Wari conquest of Nasca civilization
Science.summary: For centuries, historians have drawn the boundaries of where ancient people lived based on the evidence they left behind. By studying their remains, burial practices and other archaeological clues, they can determine the types of relationships they had with other people in the area. However, this can all change when new archaeological evidence is found.

Science.title: Population-scale immune multiome atlas reveals regulatory disease mechanisms
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11078-2 Population-scale simultaneous profiling of chromatin accessibility and gene expression across immune cells reveals regulatory architectures that connect genetic variants to disease.

Science.title: 2D semiconductor aims to turbocharge development of high-performance electronics
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02777-x An ultrathin semiconductor that conducts electricity using positively charged ‘holes’ might clear the way for next-generation electronic devices.

Science.title: Watch Live: NASA’s Crew-13 could make the fastest U.S. trip to the ISS ever
Science.summary: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission is scheduled to launch four astronauts to the International Space Station on October 1. The Dragon could reach the orbiting laboratory in just 7 hours and 50 minutes, making it the fastest U.S. spacecraft journey to the ISS in history.

Science.title: Sugar-rich foods exacerbate antibiotic-induced microbiome disruption
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11077-3 Avoiding a diet rich in simple sugars during treatment with antibiotics may mitigate microbiota disruption.

Science.title: Some threatened species may miss out as zoos try to balance conservation efforts with competing pressures
Science.summary: In the largest study of its kind, researchers at Nottingham Trent University analyzed more than 7,200 species across 613 zoos in 72 countries over a 30-year period. The team compared changes in zoo animal holdings with changes in species' conservation status, including extinction risk, international trade protections and involvement in zoo conservation breeding programs.

Science.title: Is exposomics the key to making personalized medicine a reality?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02958-8 Scientists say tailored disease treatments require a comprehensive assessment of a person’s lifelong environmental exposures.

Science.title: The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02965-9 Researchers are trying everything they can to help coral reefs to survive severe heat stress from climate change, including playing sounds underwater.

Science.title: Regular exercise reshapes the immune system at a cellular level, study suggests
Science.summary: Regular exercise makes our immune cells more vigilant, potentially contributing to better long-term health, a new study finds.

Science.title: Mulberry may reshape gut bacteria and influence metabolism
Science.summary: Mulberry compounds may reshape the gut microbiome in ways that support intestinal health and metabolism, with some combinations showing especially strong effects in animal studies. However, the results vary depending on the plant part and processing method, and the benefits have yet to be confirmed in humans.

Science.title: A TBK1/ULK1 signalling axis couples lysosomal stress to TFEB activation
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11093-3 Proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses of lysosomes identify a nutrient-independent regulatory arm of mTORC1 signalling that mediates lysosomal adaptation to stress and whose deregulation underlies tumorigenesis in follicular lymphoma.

Science.title: Trump can't stop America's shift to clean energy. And we can accelerate it.
Science.summary: The cost of clean energy just keeps falling as the price of coal ramps up. Politicians promising affordability will follow those savings no matter who is in the White House. And in the meantime, there are ways to speed up the transition, says associate professor Leah Stokes .

Science.title: Sharks can hear nearly 250 feet away and pinpoint the source
Science.summary: Wild blacktip sharks can detect low-frequency sounds from nearly 250 feet away, according to experiments conducted off the Florida coast. The sharks not only heard the sounds but sharply changed direction away from them, suggesting they could pinpoint where they were coming from.

Science.title: Why some Ukrainian refugees struggle to rebuild their careers after arriving in Canada
Science.summary: The Russian invasion of Ukraine continues into 2026, with millions of Ukrainians displaced around the world. Many arrived in host countries with professional experience, degrees and specialized skills. Yet displacement often leaves highly educated refugees unable to continue their previous careers.

Science.title: Human genetics implicates a BACH2–NRF2 axis in fetal haemoglobin activation
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11113-2 BACH2 restrains activation of the fetal-haemoglobin-encoding γ-globin genes, while loss of BACH2 enhances NRF2 chromatin occupancy and promotes the formation of activation foci at the γ-globin genes.

Science.title: This award-winning microscopy image used AI — igniting controversy in a prestigious competition
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03086-z Researchers say that using artificial-intelligence tools to visualize scientific images can become problematic when models misrepresent the underlying data.

Science.title: Beware sham scientific societies: the research community must be more vigilant
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03047-6 As AI content makes bad actors harder to spot, scrutiny of organizations must increase without reducing trust.

Science.title: Wafer-scale epitaxy growth of high-mobility p-type boron carbon nitride
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11047-9 A dual-precursor chemical system is used to achieve wafer-scale epitaxy growth of boron carbon nitride, a high-performance p-type semiconductor, for potential integration in efficient 2D materials for electronics.

Science.title: Scalable decision-making for games of imperfect information
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11036-y Ataraxos, an AI for the board wargame Stratego, establishes a design pattern for reinforcement learning and search that is effective under large amounts of hidden information, a longstanding desideratum of the field of strategic decision-making.

Science.title: I turn up late to meetings to dodge small talk. Am I wrong?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02201-4 A jury weighs in on whether a latecomer is simply using their time efficiently or disrespecting their colleagues.

Science.title: Community-led archaeology project uncovers a major monastery of medieval Scotland
Science.summary: Community-led archaeology has uncovered the remains of an early medieval monastery in Argyll, western Scotland, identifying it as the high-ranking ecclesiastical center of Lios Mòr, previously known only from historical references and local traditions.

Science.title: Classifying groundwater systems by their ability to recover from drought
Science.summary: A few days of rain do not change low groundwater levels after a long drought. To better determine how groundwater systems recover after a drought and which groundwater reserves are most vulnerable, hydrologist Sandra Hauswirth developed a method to classify groundwater systems based on their ability to recover from prolonged drought.

Science.title: Who’s the loudest of them all? The bare-throated bellbird vies for the prize
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03038-7 The bellbird’s extra-large gape helps it to achieve pneumatic-drill-level volume.

Science.title: Harmful tau spreads like self-propagating prion proteins
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02778-w Structural studies support the idea that fibrillized tau protein, a feature of neurodegenerative disorders, acts as a prion-like template to induce misfolding in healthy tau.

Science.title: The buck stops with me
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02863-0 A note to self.

Science.title: Global mangrove distribution on the open coast is controlled by waves
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11089-z A process-driven mangrove presence or absence model using 20 years of open-source wave data shows that wave conditions are critical in determining where mangroves grow worldwide.

Science.title: X-ray liquidography decodes complex motions in azobenzene isomerization
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11068-4 Time-resolved X-ray liquidography films the structural changes of azobenzene during trans-to-cis isomerization in solution with atomic-level precision.

Science.title: Carbene transfer from thianthrenium ylides for cyclopropanation
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11108-z Thianthrenium ylides can be used as a general platform for metal–carbene generation and transfer, including cyclopropanation, σ-bond insertion and sigmatropic rearrangements.

Science.title: Osteoclasts intercept meningeal lymphatic paths for dural metastasis
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11082-6 Osteoclast-derived angiopoietin-2 in the dura mater impairs lymphatic vessel function and weakens anti-tumour immunity against dural metastases, which offers new therapeutic approaches to restore meningeal lymphatic function through selective osteoclast targeting.

Science.title: Transcription pause and elongation regulators mediate somatic hypermutation
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11092-4 The molecular factors and mechanisms that mediate the chromatin recruitment of activation-induced deaminase and the generation of its stalled polymerase II substrate during somatic hypermutation are identified.

Science.title: GPCR antagonism via rewiring of receptor trafficking and degradation
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11088-0 A strategy for functional G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) antagonism through bispecific antibody-mediated endocytosis and lysosomal degradation is reported.

Science.title: Butterfly wing patterns in flight create powerful illusory motion cues
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11062-w Butterfly wing patterns and flight dynamics work in tandem to create powerful visual illusions that confuse predators, potentially representing one of the most successful visual defence strategies in moving animals.

Science.title: A two-hit mechanism triggers autoimmune hair loss
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11098-y Immune dysregulation and physiological neural activation converge to trigger autoimmune alopecia.

Science.title: Confronting demons: How acoustic and AI technology brought ancient Etruscan tombs back to life
Science.summary: Although it is not always obvious, sound guides how we experience the world around us. And the latest archaeoacoustic techniques show that even the world's earliest architects understood this.

Science.title: Secret watermark labels proteins as ‘made by AI’
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03033-y An innovative safeguard could help to flag proteins devised by artificial-intelligence tools such as AlphaFold, but the digital marker can be erased.

Science.title: Cloudflare plans to issue quantum-safe TLS certificates
Science.summary: The move will be part of a major overhaul of the ecosystem for website authentication.

Science.title: Fine-tuning cobalt for cleaner chemical transformations
Science.summary: Finding alternatives to precious metals in chemical manufacturing may be less like sourcing a substitute and more like tuning an instrument already in hand.

Science.title: Celebrity Traitors: Research suggests that some contestants will find the game tougher than it looks
Science.summary: "The Traitors" has become essential viewing for millions of fans. The TV game show, in which a group of "faithfuls" try to identify a smaller number of hidden traitors, is all about truth and lies.

Science.title: Tuberculosis treatment has advanced — now we need to stop drug resistance dragging us backwards
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02963-x The next major advancement in TB might not be a new drug, but a better understanding of how and why resistance to medicines emerges.

Science.title: Powerful 'Kelvin wave' triggered by super El Niño threatens to raise sea levels off the California coast for months
Science.summary: A disturbance characterized by above-normal sea levels is spreading up the Pacific coast of Central and North America, and it could make the damage from predicted storms this winter much worse.

Science.title: Creatine may help build muscle even without exercise, researchers find
Science.summary: Creatine helped middle-aged adults gain muscle and strength even without a structured workout program in a new 12-week study. When combined with exercise and a calorie-reduced diet, it produced even greater strength gains while helping participants add lean tissue and lose fat. Researchers say the results strengthen the case for creatine as a potentially useful tool for maintaining muscle with age.

Science.title: Short on time? It could be good for you
Science.summary: When it comes to mental health, it may not be how much time you have that matters, but rather how you feel about the time you have. That's one key takeaway of a new University of Colorado Boulder study examining the relationship between time and mental health.
